title: Repentigny police shooting: 'I called for help, but they killed my son'
subtitle: The shooting of Jean-René Olivier, who was in crisis, follows years of difficult relations between local cops and Black residents.
article: A day after Repentigny police fatally shot her son, Marie-Mireille Bence stood outside her home and shook her head in anger as she demanded answers.
Surrounded by grieving family members, Bence asked how police officers could shoot a man in distress and said as a Black woman, she no longer feels safe calling 911.
"I called for help, but they killed my son," Bence told reporters on Monday, insisting he wasn't a threat to anyone.
"It's absurd. There were other ways of controlling him, but they didn't use them. They took his life."
Jean-René Olivier, 38, was in crisis early Sunday when Bence called the police. Her son had a small knife on him and was talking about people around him wanting to hurt him.
Bence feared her son was going to hurt himself, she said. She called police when family members couldn't get through to him.
Quebec's Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), which investigates police interventions in the province, has taken over the investigation.
In a brief statement, the agency said Olivier fled by foot after officers tried to convince him to drop the knife.

Olivier then became threatening, the agency said, at which point officers unsuccessfully used pepper spray before firing several shots. According to members of the family, Olivier had dropped the knife before being shot three times.
"All we want is answers. The question is, why three bullets? My father wasn't threatening," Olivier's 18-year-old son, Kayshawn, said on Monday.
"Three bullets in the chest and we don't know why," he said. "Now we're on our own, me and my brother."

The shooting follows years of difficult relations between the Repentigny police force and Black residents. Many said it's now reignited the community's concerns that nothing has changed within the force despite several public promises to do better.

About 40 kilometres north of Montreal, the city made headlines in 2019 when a group of Black residents called on the Quebec government to launch an inquiry into the police department following several instances of alleged racial profiling.

The same groups reiterated Monday that a larger probe into the department is still needed. They said little has been done to address residents' fears since then and noted there are still four ongoing human rights complaints over alleged instances of racial profiling.

"We saw this coming and it could have been prevented," said Hèzu Kpowbié, a Black man who police surrounded at gunpoint two years ago as his young son watched. "A year ago I asked the mayor to act before someone dies. Now, unfortunately, a man has died. It's enough."

During a news conference outside the Repentigny police station Monday afternoon, police chief Helen Dion offered her condolences to the family and vowed to visit Bence in person to discuss what happened.

Dion said it was the first fatal intervention in the police force's history. Given the ongoing allegations of racial profiling, however, she said she knows the incident will be "particularly distressing" for Black residents.
"Despite all the training, or all the experience a police officer may have," Dion said, "believe me, none of us wakes up in the morning wanting to fire a weapon."
Dion said the force is working on strategies to better serve Black residents and rebuild bridges, "turning all stones" to ensure their interventions are free of biases or discrimination.
In terms of handling calls involving mental health crises, the force said it has a protocol in place to call in a psychosocial worker from the local health authority when needed.
But given the ongoing investigation, it wouldn't say whether that was done on Sunday or discuss what steps were taken before Olivier was shot.
Among the family members who had gathered earlier was Dolmine Laguerre, Olivier's cousin. As Bence spoke, Laguerre stood behind her holding a knife similar to the one Olivier had on Sunday.
"We want answers from the police chief, we want answers from the mayor," she later told reporters. "One little knife and six police can't contain him?"
Laguerre said as a mother herself, she no longer feels Repentigny is a safe place for her children to grow up because "our skin colour speaks for us."
As she spoke, she apologized several times for growing angry. But she called on everyone to understand what the family is living through.
"They killed him and now we need to bury a mother's son," she said of Olivier.
"Look at this woman, in one day, she lost everything. Just in one day," Laguerre added, pointing back toward Bence. "If it was your son, your brother, your sister... how would you feel today?"
